Daniel’s framing usefully pits “convenience” against “consistency,” but it quietly treats consistency as “always the same default selection,” when in UI practice the deeper value is *predictability with legible rules*. A “last used” default can be perfectly consistent if the rule is obvious, discoverable, and signposted; the failure mode isn’t change per se, it’s *opaque state*. This is close to Jakob Nielsen’s heuristics around visibility of system status and consistency/standards ([Nielsen Norman Group – 10 Usability Heuristics](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)): the user should be able to anticipate what Enter will do *without having to visually re-parse the list every time*. Solution B becomes costly when the state is hidden or when the consequence of a mis-hit is high (connecting to the wrong cluster, running jobs in the wrong environment, etc.).

That’s also why Solution C, while appealing, may be more fragile than it looks: a “most frequent in the last six” rule is hard to infer, easy to mispredict when habits shift, and can produce surprising defaults after a brief burst of atypical usage. It risks the worst of both worlds—neither a stable anchor like #0 nor an easily understood “last used”—because the user must reverse-engineer a probabilistic model. If WinSCP does anything like this, it would be strengthened by making the logic explicit (e.g., a visible “Default: Most used recently” label, or an affordance to pin a session), which echoes Don Norman’s emphasis on making system mappings and intentions understandable rather than magical ([*The Design of Everyday Things*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Design_of_Everyday_Things)).

The accessibility point is the most important expansion Daniel hints at but doesn’t fully cash out: keyboard and screen-reader users don’t just need a stable default; they need *low-cost verification* and *error tolerance*. A practical synthesis is: default to last used (simple rule), but provide a one-keystroke “connect to pinned/favorite server,” clear focus indication, and an opt-in setting for “always start at top.” That shifts the question from “Which single default is best?” to “How does the UI support different working patterns (alternating morning/evening, multiple projects) without forcing visual checking or repeated navigation?”
